10=10.11|12=12.5.description: The Rails monolith would access repositories through local-disk copies treated as reconstructible warm caches rather than fixed authoritative replicas. If a cache failed, repository state would need to be reconstructed, although these choices do not specify the authoritative source or the client-side scaling mechanisms used.

10=10.11|12=12.5|9=9.1.description: A Rails monolith provides the primary centralized repository access service, while local disk repositories serve as warm, reconstructible caches of repository data rather than authoritative replicas. This combines centralized control with cache-based resilience: disk copies can be rebuilt after failure without being treated as the durable source of truth.

10=10.12|11=11.14|9=9.11.description: Repositories are explicitly registered to activate local configuration and background performance maintenance, while any absent copy is reconstructed on demand from durable log state. Reconstructed repositories use delta-compressed packfile storage, reducing storage requirements but potentially adding read hops.

10=10.15|12=12.12.description: The system validates replica freshness with conditional object-store metadata checks before serving repository reads, helping ensure clients access current durable copies. On the client, a Git-aware filesystem watcher monitors relevant working-tree changes while respecting repository exclusions, reducing unnecessary event processing; the two mechanisms address different layers and are compatible.

10=10.15|6=6.7.description: Replicas use conditional object-store metadata checks to verify freshness before serving repository reads, while pushes and other fundamental operations are processed in a single consistent order. The freshness check supports read correctness, but by itself does not establish the ordering or acknowledgment behavior for writes.

10=10.1|11=11.24|12=12.3.description: The system distributes repository replicas across racks to withstand rack- and node-level failures, while servers use quiesced rolling reboots to maintain service during sequential maintenance within bounded failure domains. Clients use compressed Git indexes to reduce local repository metadata size, complementing the server-side durability and operational scaling.

10=10.1|6=6.4.description: The system places repository replicas across separate racks, so copies remain available through individual-node or rack-level failures. Its write policy accepts changes only with a permanent data-loss guarantee, ensuring accepted pushes, merges, edits, and repository creations are not corrupted or reverted.

10=10.21|11=11.2|6=6.28.description: The system can deploy any number of read replicas to scale read-only repository operations, while prioritizing user-initiated reference updates over maintenance bookkeeping. Reference changes are handled as tentative transactions and rolled back completely if they fail; the choices are compatible, although replica update or read-consistency behavior is not specified.

10=10.26|11=11.10|6=6.13.description: The system would keep filesystem replicas co-located, continuously track repository-copy validity, and use checksums to prioritize repairs, while allowing any healthy server to accept pushes through durable compare-and-swap synchronization without leader election. The co-located placement is marked rejected, so this topology is not an endorsed final choice even though it can operate with the accepted repair and write policies.

10=10.27|6=6.2|9=9.1.description: A centralized repository service would serve as the primary access point, persisting write-ahead logs on an S3 Express low-latency object-storage tier for high-throughput repository state durability. It would favor consistency and partition tolerance, acknowledging writes only when those guarantees can be maintained and refusing or delaying them when conflicts arise, reducing availability during partitions.

10=10.9|11=11.30|6=9.7.description: A proxy forwards each Git push to multiple repository replicas, whose storage can be managed through replaceable JGit repository-storage interfaces while preserving Git operations. The service can mark a node advisory-offline after approximately three consecutive failed operations, affecting subsequent routing or maintenance; no explicit write-acknowledgment or refusal behavior is specified.

10=12.18|6=6.3|9=9.12.description: The system exposes repositories through Git packfile-based networking while maintaining incremental commit-graph files for reachable commits, reducing repeated graph-update cost. Repository writes are accepted only after synchronous commitment establishes the required durability guarantee; these choices have no evident conflict.

10=12.27|6=6.17.description: The system would deploy GVFS without the cache-server infrastructure needed to support sufficiently large repositories, while requiring each repository write to acquire an exclusive majority lock. This provides a majority-based safeguard against conflicting writes, but the lack of cache infrastructure may limit scalability or suitability for large repositories.

11=10.2|12=12.22.description: The system provides each repository with at least three server-side copies, supporting redundancy and capacity after one machine fails. Clients separately perform pack rewriting and deletion of obsolete packs as distinct maintenance operations; these choices address complementary server and client concerns without evident tension.

11=11.13|12=12.31.description: Repository-service scaling would be implemented in and contributed to upstream Git, reducing reliance on specialized clients over time. Client maintenance would use single-pack full repacking as stated, but because that choice is rejected, it is not an accepted or fully coherent part of the resulting design.

11=11.18|6=6.23|9=9.1.description: The system uses centralized repository hosting as the primary access point, with automatic repair of unhealthy or lagging replicas to restore redundancy and service capacity. Foreground automatic garbage collection is rejected, so repository commands do not synchronously trigger garbage collection under this design.

11=11.22|12=12.23|6=6.6.description: The platform supports low-friction repository migration, while client-side object-database cleanup runs in the background to avoid blocking routine Git commands. Repository writes are acknowledged only after their operations are durably recorded in the WAL, providing a clear durability guarantee alongside migration and maintenance scalability.

11=11.26|12=12.25|9=9.16.description: An application layer over unmodified Git repositories could manage service operations by quiescing planned-maintenance servers for new reads while existing reads drain. Clients would perform incremental repacks by selecting only a bounded set of small packfiles, limiting each maintenance operation’s scope.

11=11.9|12=12.11.description: A core Git client with standardized GVFS protocol support would access large repositories through co-located transfer-cache proxies, which serve repeated large-object requests near users and build machines. This combines a common client-side access mechanism with server-side caching to reduce repeated transfer costs; the combination is conceptually compatible, though the GVFS choice has mixed status.

12=12.20|9=9.3.description: Clients use incremental bounded pack repacking to keep local repository maintenance costs controlled as data grows. The repositories themselves are distributed through the filesystem layer across application instances, preserving existing Rails and Git internals; these choices address different scaling concerns and are compatible.

12=12.29|6=6.25|9=9.12.description: A Git-based system would support very large repositories through client-side scaling optimizations without requiring a virtualized filesystem, while transferring repository data using Git packfiles. Repository writes would be evaluated across replicas with deterministic reference-update results, providing consistent acknowledgment or refusal behavior.

12=12.3|6=6.13.description: Clients use a compressed Git index to reduce local repository metadata while performing normal working-tree operations. Pushes may target any healthy repository primary without leader election; durable compare-and-swap synchronization coordinates concurrent updates, while the client-side index optimization remains independent of server write-consistency policy.

12=12.4|9=9.14.description: A Git-level distribution system would modify or distribute Git itself rather than replicate repository data above Git. Client repositories could use Git’s built-in filesystem monitor to accelerate status and add operations across large working trees; the choices address different layers and are compatible.

6=6.17|9=9.6.description: The system would require each repository write to obtain an exclusive lock from a majority before accepting it, preventing conflicting writes from being committed concurrently. Once authorized, the write’s content-addressed objects would be distributed individually across storage nodes rather than kept in repository-level packfiles; these choices are compatible, although the storage representation is marked rejected.
